strengths: Addresses important and well-motivated gap in molecule-language interfaces with clear real-world relevance
Exceptionally rigorous dataset construction with multi-stage annotation pipeline (writing → peer review → dual independent validation) ensuring unambiguous ground truth
Comprehensive evaluation spanning 13+ LLMs and vision-language models with variance analysis and prompt sensitivity studies
Identifies important failure modes and insights: BPE tokenization issues, 10%+ recognition-localization gap, assembly failures in generation, ineffectiveness of vision representations
Excellent reproducibility: detailed prompts, model snapshots, promised public release, comprehensive supplementary materials
Supports multiple molecular representations (SMILES, images, graphs) and includes both core and extended datasets
Well-presented with clear task formulation and extensive visual examples
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily a dataset paper using standard annotation methodologies without algorithmic or methodological innovations expected for top-tier venues
Modest dataset scale (200-400 instances per task, 3,600 total recognition instances) relative to modern benchmarks; insufficient for training large models

Incomplete evaluation scope: graph-language models acknowledged as unavailable; chemistry-specific models (ChemDFM, ChemLLM, Galactica) relegated to appendix despite failing completely (0-2.5% accuracy), their failure remains unexplained

Shallow error analysis: identifies problems without actionable solutions; tokenization issue noted but not explored for solutions (e.g., character-level tokenization); generation assembly failures noted without categorization
No inter-annotator agreement metrics despite multi-annotator pipeline; missing confidence intervals and statistical significance testing

Unclear image representation validity: images generated from SMILES rather than authentic chemical drawings; no exploration of alternative 2D/3D representations; no validation that visual representation was appropriate choice
Dataset composition concerns: <40 atom restriction not justified; no difficulty distribution analysis; generalization to larger molecules unexplored; UniChem sourcing biases unexamined
Extended set quality unvalidated: simplified pipeline (1 annotator + 1 validator) creates unknown accuracy degradation vs. core set; results primarily on core set only
Limited comparative context: minimal discussion of existing molecule-language datasets; no user study validating task relevance for chemists; no guidance for practitioners on model improvements
Dramatic performance variance across editing task categories (30-100% accuracy by category, Table S2) remains unexplained and suggests potential design issues or exceptionally hard subcategories

strengths: Exceptionally rigorous dataset construction with multi-stage annotation pipeline, peer review, and independent validation ensuring high-quality deterministic outputs
Comprehensive evaluation spanning 15+ diverse models (general-purpose LLMs, reasoning-specialized, vision-language) with honest reporting of limitations
Well-motivated tasks grounded in real chemistry workflows (recognition, editing, generation) with clear practical relevance

Detailed error analysis revealing systematic failure modes (tokenization issues causing atom enumeration errors, stereochemistry recognition failures, chain length mistakes) with concrete mechanistic insights
Multiple modality support (SMILES, molecular images, graphs) and thorough supplementary analyses (prompt sensitivity, variance analysis, SELFIES evaluation, chemistry-specific LLM evaluation)
Clear identification of significant limitations even in state-of-the-art models (GPT-5: 86.2% recognition, 43% generation) providing valuable benchmarking resource
Reproducibility considerations including model snapshots, variance analysis, and promised release of dataset and code
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale with only 200 core examples per task raises questions about statistical significance and generalization; lacks analysis of dataset size sufficiency
Circular task design for recognition: using RDKit to generate ground truth then evaluating LLMs on RDKit-solvable tasks limits clarity on meaningful reasoning evaluation
Small molecule complexity scope (mostly <40 non-H atoms) insufficient for real pharmaceutical compounds; lacks evaluation on truly complex polycyclic systems
Extensive documentation of failure modes but limited mechanistic analysis or proposed solutions; no experiments with potential improvements (chain-of-thought, few-shot learning, fine-tuning)

Vision-language evaluation concerns: GPT Image 1 performs catastrophically (0% generation) with limited analysis; only one image model evaluated; overlaid atom indices may not reflect realistic scenarios
Weak practical motivation: unclear when chemists would use LLMs to recognize structures they already possess; limited connection between solving tasks and downstream chemistry applications
Limited novelty: primarily engineering/curation contribution rather than methodological innovation; task formulation is relatively straightforward application of existing concepts
Missing key baselines and comparisons: no traditional chemistry software baselines, simple heuristics, retrieval methods, or systematic analysis of why chemistry-specific LLMs fail dramatically
Evaluation strictness concerns: exact SMILES match is overly stringent given multiple valid representations exist; Tanimoto similarity deemphasized; OCR has 2.7% false positive rate
Modest downstream improvements with structure analysis (~5% on BBBP/BACE) and limited evidence that solving MolLangBench enables real scientific applications
